subject: Cognitive Science
title: When Intuition Works
description: A quick, practical guide to When Intuition Works.

hook.text: A firefighter yells "Get out!" moments before a floor collapses. He can't explain how he knew. But he knew.

buildup.text: Gary Klein studied expert intuition: in high-validity environments, experienced people recognize patterns fast.

discovery.text: Intuition works when the environment is regular, there's practice, and feedback is rapid and clear.

twist.text: In low-validity domains—stock markets, political forecasts—intuition fails. The patterns are illusions.

climax.text: Kahneman and Klein agreed: trust intuition in chess and firefighting, not in hiring and investing.

punchline.text: Trust your gut only where patterns are real.

quiz.question: When does expert intuition work best?
options: In regular environments with rapid, clear feedback

details.summary: Intuition is reliable when it draws on genuine expertise in a domain with regular, learnable patterns and where the expert has received clear feedback. The intuitions of experienced firefighters and nurses are often trustworthy. Intuition in unpredictable domains like stock markets is not.
details.whyItMatters: Knowing when to trust intuition and when to demand analysis prevents both reckless gut decisions and paralyzing overthinking.
takeaways: Intuition is reliable in regular domains with clear feedback
Expert intuition is pattern recognition, not magical insight

faq.question: How can you tell if a domain supports reliable intuition?
faq.answer: Kahneman and Klein agreed on two conditions: the environment must have learnable regularities, and the expert must have had prolonged practice with feedback. Chess, firefighting, and nursing meet these conditions. Stock picking, long-term political forecasting, and hiring do not.

faq.question: Should you ever ignore your intuition?
faq.answer: Yes, when operating outside your domain of expertise, when the environment is unpredictable, or when you have not received clear feedback on similar past decisions. In these cases, structured analysis, checklists, and algorithms outperform intuition.
